fieldRequirements.value: Christianity lacks adequate rational warrant because established facts are not connected to its supernatural conclusions with sufficient specificity and comparative force.
Without independent event confirmation and a discriminating causal link, Christianity’s reports and compatible observations remain inadequate warrant for its supernatural core.

finalArgument.thesis: Christianity lacks adequate rational warrant because established facts are not connected to its supernatural conclusions with sufficient specificity and comparative force.
premises: Internal coherence and practical usefulness cannot establish actuality, because coherent fictions and beneficial institutions may remain false about their underlying explanations.
Historical reports gain weight through provenance, independence, adverse attestation, and corroboration, but accurate textual preservation alone does not verify narrated events.
Even an extraordinary observed event would not establish divine agency unless evidence discriminated that cause from error, legend, psychology, or unknown nature.
Cooperation, sacrifice, hope, and religious desire possess natural and cultural explanations, making their compatibility with Christianity weak and nonspecific confirmation.
Biblical violence, eternal punishment, and forgiveness create unresolved proportional-justice tensions that weaken Christianity’s claim to a uniquely coherent divine moral character.
finalArgument.conclusion: Without independent event confirmation and a discriminating causal link, Christianity’s reports and compatible observations remain inadequate warrant for its supernatural core.

newArguments.title: Likelihood-ratio challenge
newArguments.text: Dillahunty could ask how probable every cited fact is under Christianity compared with ordinary historical and psychological alternatives. Observations predicted by both sides should contribute little evidential weight. This approach replaces categorical claims of no evidence with the more defensible conclusion that the offered evidence has low discriminatory value, directly answering cumulative reasoning on its own probabilistic terms.

newArguments.title: Source-dependence audit
newArguments.text: The con case could apply its historical criteria to the alleged six resurrection sources by identifying dates, authorship, literary relationships, eyewitness access, genre, interests, and genuinely independent details. Adjusting the apparent count for common dependence would reveal whether multiplicity corroborates an event or repeats a developing tradition. That audit would strengthen the critique without treating all testimony as categorically worthless.

newArguments.title: Divine communication prediction
newArguments.text: Hiddenness could be framed as a comparative prediction rather than a demand about what God must do. A loving communicative God seeking relationship should make sincere inquiry reliably converge on recognizable access, while knowledge need not compel loyalty. Persistent culturally patterned disagreement among nonresistant inquirers would then be more expected under human religious construction, providing positive contrary evidence rather than merely noting an unmet burden.

frozenMoves.proposition: Because Christianity posits a communicative agent able to supply a rational model but no such evidential explanation has appeared, its burden of proof remains unmet.

frozenMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
frozenMoves.proposition: Secular humanism does not assume innate human goodness, and cooperation, sympathy, and forgiveness can arise through practical problem-solving and game-theoretic interdependence.

frozenMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
frozenMoves.proposition: Even if Christianity improved society, usefulness would not make belief in its core supernatural claims rational.

frozenMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
frozenMoves.proposition: Religious desires and facts compatible with Christianity do not support it unless evidence links Christianity's proposed explanation to those facts.

frozenMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty

frozenMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty

frozenMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
frozenMoves.proposition: Whether a belief is rational can differ between people because evidentiary warrant depends on the evidence available to each person, even if the underlying proposition has one objective truth value.

frozenMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
frozenMoves.proposition: Historical evidence need not be empirically verifiable, and its strength can increase with multiple sources, especially when competing parties independently report consistent facts.
